entities.evidence: אֱלֹהִים is the subject of the singular verb וַיֹּאמֶר. The speaker is the God who creates in Genesis 1, matching the existing source tag.

name_review_base.evidence: אֱלֹהִים is the subject of the singular verb וַיֹּאמֶר. The speaker is the God who creates in Genesis 1, matching the existing source tag.

review.translation: [Then|0] [God|1] [said|0], “[Let us make|2] [humankind|3] [in our image|4], [according to our likeness|5], [and let them rule|6] [over the fish of|7] [the sea|8], [and over the bird{s} of|9] [the sky|10], [and over the livestock|11], [and over all|12] [the earth|13], [and over every|14] [creeping creature|15] [that moves|16] [on|17] [the ground|18].”

analysis.evidence: אֱלֹהִים is the subject of וַיֹּאמֶר. The first-person plural נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם (“let us make humankind”) opens God's direct speech.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־

analysis.evidence: The singular verb וַיֹּאמֶר (“he said”) presents אֱלֹהִים as one speaker. The plural נַעֲשֶׂה (“let us make”) begins God’s quoted speech.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural common noun in the absolute state, with singular verbal agreement.

analysis.evidence: In God’s speech, אָדָם is the direct object of נַעֲשֶׂה. The phrases בְּצַלְמֵנוּ and כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ describe how humankind is to be made and echo the verb’s first-person plural with “our image” and “our likeness.”
analysis.morphology: Qal imperfect, first person common plural, with cohortative force

analysis.evidence: אָדָם is the object of נַעֲשֶׂה, “let us make.” The plural וְיִרְדּוּ, “and let them rule,” refers back to the humans being created, showing that the singular noun has collective sense.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the absolute state, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: God says נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם ‘let us make humankind’. The parallel phrase כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ ‘according to our likeness’ clarifies that ‘our image’ expresses the likeness humankind is to bear to its maker.
analysis.morphology: Preposition בְּ ‘in’ + masculine singular construct noun + first-person common plural possessive suffix ־ֵנוּ ‘our’.

analysis.evidence: כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ parallels בְּצַלְמֵנוּ ‘in our image’. Both phrases describe how God proposes to make humankind, and both carry the suffix meaning ‘our’.
analysis.morphology: Preposition כְּ ‘according to’ + feminine singular construct noun דְּמוּת + first-person common plural possessive suffix ־ֵנוּ ‘our’.

analysis.evidence: Following נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם (“let us make humankind”), the plural וְיִרְדּוּ refers to humankind collectively. The repeated preposition בְּ introduces those over whom they are to rule, beginning with the fish of the sea and the birds of the heavens.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וְ prefixed to a Qal jussive, third person masculine plural.

analysis.evidence: In וְיִרְדּוּ בִדְגַת הַיָּם, בִ־ marks what humans are to rule over. The construct דְגַת takes הַיָּם as its complement, giving “the fish of the sea,” parallel to “the birds of the heavens.”
analysis.morphology: Prefixed preposition בְּ (surface בִ־) + feminine singular construct noun דְגַת, used collectively.

analysis.evidence: In בִדְגַת הַיָּם, “the fish of the sea,” הַיָּם names the fish’s habitat, parallel to הַשָּׁמַיִם in “the birds of the heavens.”
analysis.morphology: Definite article הַ־ prefixed to a masculine singular absolute noun.

analysis.evidence: וּבְעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם means ‘and over the birds of the sky’. It parallels בִדְגַת הַיָּם ‘over the fish of the sea’ in the list of creatures governed by וְיִרְדּוּ ‘let them rule’.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular collective noun in the construct state, prefixed by וּ־ ‘and’ and בְּ־ ‘over’ with the verb רדה.

analysis.evidence: The phrase וּבְעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם, “and over the birds of the sky,” parallels בִדְגַת הַיָּם, “over the fish of the sea.” Each phrase names the animals’ habitat.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הַ־ prefixed to a masculine plural noun in the absolute state.

analysis.evidence: The verb וְיִרְדּוּ governs the repeated preposition בְּ, introducing each group over which humans are to rule. The singular בְּהֵמָה designates livestock collectively, alongside the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, and the creatures that creep on the ground.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וּ followed by the preposition בְּ with the definite article (בַּ) and a feminine singular absolute noun used collectively.

analysis.evidence: In וּבְכָל הָאָרֶץ, כָל takes the definite singular הָאָרֶץ as its complement. The phrase means “and over the whole earth,” expressing the full extent of the dominion described by וְיִרְדּוּ.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular construct noun with prefixed conjunction וּ־ and preposition בְּ־.

analysis.evidence: In וּבְכָל הָאָרֶץ, “and over all the earth,” כָל gives הָאָרֶץ its full scope as a domain of human rule under וְיִרְדּוּ.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, common gender, singular absolute, with prefixed definite article הָ־.

analysis.evidence: וְיִרְדּוּ ‘let them rule’ governs the preposition בְּ־. כָל quantifies the collective singular הָרֶמֶשׂ, so the phrase includes every creeping thing that moves on the earth.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וּ־ ‘and’ + preposition בְּ־ ‘over’ + masculine singular construct noun כָל.

analysis.evidence: After וּבְכָל, הָרֶמֶשׂ names a class of creatures under human rule, alongside fish, birds, and livestock. The following participle הָרֹמֵשׂ modifies the noun and describes how these creatures move on the earth.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular absolute common noun with the prefixed definite article הָ־, used collectively.

analysis.evidence: הָרֹמֵשׂ agrees with the definite masculine singular collective noun הָרֶמֶשׂ. The following עַל הָאָרֶץ specifies where the creatures move, “on the earth.”
analysis.morphology: Definite article הָ־ + Qal active participle, masculine singular absolute, used attributively.

analysis.evidence: In הָרֹמֵשׂ עַל הָאָרֶץ, “that creeps on the earth,” עַל introduces the surface on which the creature moves.
In הָרֹמֵשׂ עַל הָאָרֶץ, “that creeps on the ground,” עַל introduces the surface on which the creature moves.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, singular absolute, with the prefixed definite article הָ־.
